narrative:
The model estimated a 69.0% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, and because that risk exceeded the admission threshold, your law school application was denied. This is a risk estimate, not a judgment that you cannot succeed.

The denial was driven most strongly by your undergraduate GPA. At 2.60, it is below the 3.23 average among accepted students, and this was the largest factor pushing the prediction toward bar-exam failure. The second strongest factor was your family income bracket: being in the middle-income group, compared with the accepted pool where upper-middle income is most common, also pushed the estimate toward failure. The third strongest factor was your LSAT score. Your 34 is below the accepted-student average of 37.18, which likewise increased the predicted risk. Together, these signals outweighed the parts of your profile that were more favorable.

Next, ask admissions whether the decision can be reconsidered or whether conditional admission is available. If possible, retake the LSAT after preparation, provide evidence of improved academic performance through additional coursework, and request an advising meeting to discuss a concrete bar-prep plan. You may also apply to schools that review applicants more holistically or offer academic support, and explain any context behind your GPA or LSAT that the numbers do not capture.
